Spelling Bee's using graphs 

I noticed that the easiest spelling words are terms that have four letters and have been used/known for a long time. I also caught how the words usually have an O used once or twice. The Hardest Spelling words have more lettering like 5-10 letters in each. I'm curious if students get the option to have a cheat sheet or study guide where they get to study. Something that also got me wondering is if the players who participated could speak other languages. Is English their first speech? Most English words have silent letters or different spelling than how it's said. I think that spelling is something everyone struggles with at one point. Like I said before some words have a weird spelling form than how it's spoken and can make it difficult to write. Once students grow up spelling becomes a job that is meant to be developing over time. Mostly in their school life, it can be hard if they see others succeeding and they're falling behind and feel ashamed to ask for help.

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
According to the graph, I noticed that “Trigram” (16%), “Tangram” (19%), and “Trimaran” (26%), were the hardest words to guess within the spelling bee. While the easiest words to guess were “Hook” (99%), “Fork” (99%), and “Whipping” (99%). I also noticed that the level of difficulty correlates with the number of letters within the word, It appears that words containing four letters were easier to guess than words with 6-8 letters.
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder how many participants there were in this particular survey and their backgrounds, specifically the languages they speak to try and figure out if there’s a connection to the words that were accurately guessed. I’m also curious to find out if there’s a definite connection between the length of words and the percentage of guesses. 
3. What impact does this have on you and your community?
This graph shows that looking at society as a whole, we have not expanded our vocabulary beyond simple words used in daily conversation. I view the spelling bee game as a way for people to expand their knowledge and enlighten those around them with a deeper understanding of language and word use.
4. Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

raw_comment: The graph displays the percentage of people finding complicated vs uncomplicated words in the daily NYT spelling bee. It depicts how people struggle to look past a basic vocabulary when challenged. Some of the least common words are not overly obscure but are also not common words. When put on the spot many people struggle to look past their basics and experiment with words. It is natural to lean toward the easiest options at first, hence it is not a surprise that basic words are much more common than more complex vocabulary. I wonder how hard people try to find the more complicated words. I play the spelling bee sometimes and I am terrible at it because I also struggle to find the more complex words. I often mix random letters and miraculously come across difficult words. I wonder how many of these words were found that way as well. A headline for the graph would be "What the NYT spelling bee really tells us about how well we know English."

raw_comment:
What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

Comparing both graphs, the percentage range of the Hardest Spelling Bee Words (16%-39%) is much lower and has more variation than the range of the Easiest  Spelling Bee Words (98%-99%) The words on the left are not as common as those on the right; the words on the right have simple structures and on average, are shorter than most of the words on the right. The words on the left are also more obscure and not used by the average person as often. 

What do you wonder?

I wonder if the age of the person impacts what words they are able to find. Realistically teenagers and above are playing this game, so I wonder if the teens are able to think more creatively or if adults have a better grasp on the English language. I also wonder if where the person lives affects their knowledge, some words are used more often in English speaking countries, and those who are from non-english countries might only know simple structures. 

What impact does this have on you and your community?

Many of the Students at AOSE play these and other NYT games, and looking at the words I've been able to find, usually I find words that I'm more familiar with. 

Catchy Headline:

Can you spell these Un-BEE-lievable words?

raw_comment:
The first graph illustrates the New York Times spelling bee game’s most difficult words, while the second graph depicts the more easily discoverable ones. The yellow bars on each graph indicate the percentage of words that each contestant was able to identify and correctly spell. 

A noticeable trend emerged when analyzing these graphs: shorter, more common words that are frequently encountered in daily life were associated with a significantly higher success, with an average of 98% participants correctly identifying four-letter common words. In contrast, a mere 16% of individuals managed to identify the longer, less common, and more difficult words.  

This intriguing pattern poses the question to consider whether age might be a factor in an individual’s ability in this game and can even be generalized to the influence of age on an individual’s ability to recognize varying difficulty of words. My hypothesis is that older adults, having been exposed to more verbiage throughout their lifetime, might find it less challenging to decipher longer, less common words due to their broader range of vocabulary. 

The relevance of this observation does extend to my personal life and community involvement, since my father is an avid player of the New York Times spelling bee game. 

Title: “When spelling BEES run out of juice”

raw_comment: In this graph, it is comparing the 10 hardest versus the 10 easiest spelling bee words for the New York Times’ Spelling Bee puzzle and the percentage of players who were able to find each word. When looking at the two different graphs in comparison with one another, I noticed that the share of players finding each word for the 10 easiest words was significantly higher than the general share of players finding each word for the 10 hardest words. The highest percentage for players finding the words for the 10 easiest words was 99% compared with 39% for the 10 hardest words, displaying a significant gap. Additionally, I noticed that with the 10 easiest words, the majority of them, with the exception of “whipping”, were 4-letter words, whereas the 10 hardest words all had a minimum of 5 letters with the longest word having 10 letters. I wonder if there is a negative correlation between the word length and the percentage of players finding each word. Although this is the case for many of the words, there are a couple exceptions such as “whipping” having a 99% finding rate and “grammarian” having the highest finding rate out of the hardest words. This relates to my community because many people I know enjoy playing New York Times games dealing with vocabulary, but this demonstrates that our vocabulary is still very limited. My headline for this graph would be: “New York Times’ Game Spelling Bee Reveals The Complexity of Our Vocabulary”.

raw_comment:
The New York Times has become not only known for being a top contending news outlet but also for its online games. The Spelling Bee, a daily challenge in which players recieve a series of seven letters and must find as many word combinations as possible, has become one of the most played NYT games. This graph shows the percentage of players that discover easier versus harder words during the daily challenges from September 23rd to the 29th. Between 98% to 99% of players spelled the top 10 easiest words. Nine out of these ten words contain four letters, with "whipping" being the exception. As for the top ten hardest words, the percentages range from 16%, the number 1 hardest word “trigram”, to 39%, the tenth hardest word “grammarian”. I wonder why certain words, such as “clade”, are harder for people to spell. While it is not necessarily a word one hears every day, it is not a complex word to write. My community, and surrounding regions in New Jersey, is known for an amazing education system both public and private. Throughout my schooling, many of my teachers have been keen on the usage of vocabulary. So, I wonder how well I, and the other students in my community, would perform on the Spelling-Bee. Would a high percentage of us be able to reach the hardest word? Within the classroom, games such as Spelling Bee could be a fun way for students to improve their spelling and vocab abilities. 


This "Spelling Bee" Means Serious BEEs-ness!

raw_comment:
I notice that the easiest spelling bee words are relatively common: fork, gone, book, and rook are all used on a somewhat frequent basis. Interestingly, 98% of players identified the top ten spelling bee words from September 23-29. A surprisingly large number of players identified at least ten words, suggesting that many players were already decent at word identification. This would skew the data, as a skilled demographic would likely perform higher overall. The hardest words were multisyllabic and less common.

I wonder if adults or students were better at the spelling bee. My guess is that adults with a communication or literature-based profession would perform better than students. However, if the adults only deal with numbers, then students may outperform them. I also wonder if people's average performance has decreased over time.

This relates to me because I enjoy doing spelling bees. However, my confidence has diminished because of the high percentage of players finding at least 10 words! This relates to my community because the low identification of more challenging vocabulary may indicate a decrease in people's lexicon. The data in the graph would have to be compared to previous spelling bees to determine a trend.

The graph depicts the hardest and easiest spelling bee words from September 23-29, demonstrating that multisyllabic, uncommon vocabulary words were less easily identified.

"When Spelling Bees Fizzle Out"

In this graph, I notice that all but one of the top 10 easiest words, were one syllable and 4 letters. The directions of the game state the word has to be at least 4 words, so most of these easiest words are the minimum. I notice that the words that were included in the 10 hardest words, were words that are not commonly used or are used in everyday life. Personally, I have not even heard of most of the words on that side. I notice that the only easiest word that is not 4 words and one syllable, is "whipping". Whipping is the verb-form of another word on this list, "whip". I wonder why that is the only verb-form of these 4 letter words on the list, and why it was not as common to add the suffix "-ing", to other eligible words, such as book or hook. This graph displays two separate bar graphs. The left bar graph depicts the 10 hardest spelling bee words from the 23-29, while the graph to the right of it provides the ten easiest spelling bee words from the same time-span. Both were measured by the percentages of people who found the words. This relates to my community, as many people play this game. It is helpful for players of the game to be aware of different patterns within finding the easiest and hardest words, as it will increase their probability of finding difficult words. 
"The key to bee-ting Spelling bee"

raw_comment:
This graph shows the results from the NYT game, Spelling Bee, and which words were the easiest and hardest to find. I notice that most of the easier words are shorter, and often involve double letters, like "OO" in "Book", "Hoof", "Rook", and "Hook". The harder words are much longer and include complex structure. The harder words are less commonly used in every day life, while most of the easier ones are. I wonder how the harder and easier words correspond to the age and education level of the players. I would assume that older, more knowledgeable and educated adults would respond with more complex words. This relates to me and my community because it shows that as humans, we tend to take the simpler route when thinking, and only a small percentage of us think deeply and critically. 
"Easy-Peasy or Brain-Teasy? "

raw_comment: The graph is depicting the percentage of NY Times' "Spelling Bee" players that discovered the hardest words versus the percentage of players that discovered the easiest words from 9/23-9/29. I noticed that there is a larger number of players that guessed the easier words. I also noticed that various of the easy words rhyme, such as "hook," "rook," and "book." Due to the similarities between these words, it is most likely a reason for the large percentage of players that guess them. I am curious about the average age of players that guessed the 10 hardest spelling bee words, in comparison to the average age of players that guessed the 10 easiest spelling bee words. Are the people that guessed words like "trigram," "tangram," and "trimaran" older, younger, or the same age as individuals that guessed the easier spelling bee words? I think that this graph impacts my community because it displays education levels and knowledge of vocabulary. If all of the people that guessed the harder spelling bee words were above a certain age group, then maybe schools should devote more time to the acquisition of vocabulary. A title for this graph would be "Spelling Bee: A Test on Your Vocabulary Knowledge."

raw_comment: The graph compares 10 of the hardest spelling bee words to the easiest from the New York Times puzzle, “Spelling Bee.” From the data, I noticed that the majority of the easier spelling bee words (in which at least 98% of players created), were 4 letters. Also, I realized that the easier spelling bee words consisted of more common words and phrases such as ‘book’ and ‘gone.’ On the other hand, the harder spelling bee words consisted of uncommon objects like ‘trimaran,’ which is a type of boat. I wonder if 4-lettered words were considered the easiest spelling bee words because people looked to create words with the minimum amount of letters. This is interesting because focusing on simplicity in making 4-lettered words results in only 1 point. In addition, I wonder what type of people were able to uncover the hardest spelling bee words and what age group performed well on the puzzle? The data from the graph relates to my community as it demonstrates how proficient Americans are in spelling and discovering challenging words.  A potential name for the graph is:  The Un-BEE-lievable Stats on The New York Times Puzzle, “Spelling Bee”

   - No stacking.
   - Bars are ordered within each panel by the percentage shown.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Word | Categorical/nominal | Y-axis position; text label beside each bar |
| Share of players finding each word (%) | Quantitative | Bar length / horizontal position; numeric label at end of bar |
| Difficulty group (Hardest vs. Easiest) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into left and right panels; panel title |
| Time period (Sept. 23–29) | Temporal | Title text |

1. I noticed that, in the graph of the 10 words that were the easiest to spell in the spelling bee, 98–99% of participants correctly spelled those words, indicating that the majority of participants were proficient spellers. In contrast, the highest percentage of participants who correctly spelled a word in the graph of the words that were the hardest was 39%. The majority of the simple words, or 90%, had four letters or fewer, whereas the hardest terms had between five and ten letters. 
2. I wonder why a relatively long and hard looking word like "whipping" is the easiest word that could be given in a spelling bee as I could think of a lot more words that would be easier. I'm also wondering about the age range of the contestants in this spelling bee as well as the quantity of sources used to arrive at these results.
3. This relates to me and my community as we are constantly having to deal with our vocabulary and knowledge of spelling. Whether it's a 2nd grade spelling bee in the auditorium, or a 10 page paper due for your literature class at the local college, Spelling and literature will always have a big effect on us. 
4. Autocorrect or The Human Brain, Has Correct Spelling Come Down To The Need of Electronics?

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
I notice that the harder words to spell have five to ten letters, and the top three hardest to spell words start with T and have many other letters in common like m, g, and a. In the top ten easiest to spell four letter words dominate and have the letter o in common. From the easiest words, the standout is whipping, the easiest to spell word, which has nothing in common with the other words (except whip). 

2) What do you wonder?
I wonder why whipping is the easiest word to spell yet has the most letters out of the top ten. I also wonder how the top three hardest to spell words have much in common. 

3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because learning English was essential to a lot of immigrants coming to the US, and a strategy me and my mom would use was to learn one word a day by doing spelling bees and other word games on our computer. Looking at the words people struggle spelling the most is interesting to me now because I see a lot of unfamiliar words and I also see some words in the easiest to spell that I used to struggle with. 

Title: Spelling Bee! Is it a Breeze or a sting?

raw_comment:
The 10 easiest spelling bee words aren't necessarily words that you would use very commonly, although they are very simple. If you think about it, when's the last time you used the words "hone" or "hoof"? Despite their lack of everyday use, I think that a few patterns in their lettering combined with their simplicity lead to making them very easy to identify on Spelling Bee. It's easier to identify words that end with a letter pattern such as "ck" or "ing" because you can predict a word much easier that way. Another pattern that I noticed in this graph is that many of the words have two of the same letter right next to each other, like "book" and "rook". Lastly, the vast majority of the easiest words are four-lettered, so they don't take a lot of time to think about. 
        On the contrary, the 10 hardest spelling bee words are the complete opposite. There isn't a single word on that graph that I would use unless in a very specific conversation, and their complete lack of patterns makes it harder to identify. The smallest word on the list is five letters, which is also something different from the easiest word graph. 

I would title this graph: "Spelling Bee Buddy is Busy"

What do you notice?
- The words that few misspelled most frequently, or were the hardest words, were the ones that didn't seem as well known. At least in my opinion, I've never heard the word coulee, or the word Toccata. I think this makes a big difference, because knowing the word means that you've been exposed to it. The easier words were one, very well known, and two, they weren't especially long.

What do you wonder?
- The first thing I wondered was how many people actually participated in the spelling bee. I think it makes a big difference because maybe the group of people was very small, meaning that there was possible under coverage in the sample. At the same time, the people doing the spelling bee might be the type of people who regularly do puzzles such as this one. I wanted to know more about the type of people participating in this spelling bee, as well how many were part of the sample. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
- This relates to the community because some of these words are used regularly. The words in the "easiest" section, are words that we see every day. I used to participate in Spelling Bees at my old school. I think it's vitally important to understand the words you're trying to spell, especially if they have different pronunciations. 

What’s going on in this graph?
The graph shows the percentages of people who spelled the words correctly.
What starts with T and is seven letters? The hardest words in this spelling bee!
